      <title>Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/26/mourinhos-plan-comes-together-as-real-madrid-relaunch-with-clasico-statement</link>
      <description><p>It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points</p><p>José Mourinho had already done the <em>por qu</em><em>é?</em>, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/21/real-madrid-atletico-madrid-jose-mourinho-diego-simeone-madrid-derby-la-liga">the printout</a> and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the <em>clásico</em> on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists.</p><p>He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/26/mourinhos-plan-comes-together-as-real-madrid-relaunch-with-clasico-statement">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Mbappé double secures Real Madrid late victory at Barcelona after Raphinha leveller</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/25/barcelona-real-madrid-el-clasico-la-liga-match-report</link>
      <description><p>Thirteen years later, José Mourinho led Real Madrid into the Camp Nou as one team and them out again as another having secured the kind of late victory he loves and which opens up a whole new world. With just three minutes and the final reserves of energy remaining, a wonderful moment of skill from Jude Bellingham found Eduardo Camavinga and set them on one last run. Camavinga sprinted free, skilfully slipped Pau Cubarsí and pulled back for Kylian Mbappé to provide the finish, a little bit of history written.</p><p>“The world that loves football will have stopped to watch this and they won’t have gone disappointed; this was two teams that played to win,” Mourinho said. It had been an intense, breathless ride, a proper battle, and it was his team who won it. Arriving right on time, Mbappé scored his second to make it 2-1, the Camp Nou falling quiet and their team given no time to react. They had drawn level after Mbappé’s opener, Raphinha scoring, but could not do it again.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/25/barcelona-real-madrid-el-clasico-la-liga-match-report">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is el clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real Madrid</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/23/el-clasico-real-madrid-barcelona-lamine-yamal-kylian-mbappe</link>
      <description><p>The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era?</p><p>For the best part of a decade, <em>el </em><em>clásico</em> was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were <em>clásicos</em> everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport.</p><p>As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the <em>clásico</em>’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a <em>clásico</em>’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture?</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/23/el-clasico-real-madrid-barcelona-lamine-yamal-kylian-mbappe">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Facing Diego Simeone 13 years on, José Mourinho brought a print-out and paranoia. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t, either</p><p>There were many questions to emerge from the Madrid derby, which <a href="http://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/20/atletico-madrid-real-madrid-la-liga-match-report">Atlético won 2-1 </a>in front of 70,514 very, very noisy people at the Metropolitano on Sunday afternoon, even if not the one José Mourinho was asking. Like: what year is this? Or: what was Dean Huijsen thinking? Why always Arda? And whatever happened to Vinícius Júnior? How come Koke is <em>still</em> the best? And how long before Giuliano Simeone <em>actually</em> bursts, his <em>atlético</em> insides exploding across the pitch? Above all though, you were left wondering: where did Real Madrid’s manager get a printer from? And how did he get the bloody thing to work?</p><p>You could still hear the singing outside when Mourinho turned up in the press room, laid down his glasses and sat. In his hand was a piece of paper. Thirteen years after his last derby, on the Santiago Bernabéu night when <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2013/may/18/atletico-madrid-real-copa-del-rey">Madrid lost the Copa del Rey final</a> and a <em>13-year</em> unbeaten run against their neighbours, Diego Simeone had defeated him again. The stage was new – <a href="http://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2017/sep/18/a-stadium-called-wanda-opening-night-at-atletico-madrids-new-home">this stadium didn’t exist then</a> – but his adversary was somehow still the same man, still dressed in black, and the scene was a bit like old times, a classic. Mourinho unfolded the paper and held it up. “We can save ourselves the bother of the press conference,” he said, “because the story is right here.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/21/real-madrid-atletico-madrid-jose-mourinho-diego-simeone-madrid-derby-la-liga">Continue reading...</a></description>
